caption: Left vs right heart failure. Left sided failure backs blood up into the lungs: dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, S3. Right sided failure backs blood up into the body: JVD, liver congestion, leg edema. The most common cause of right heart failure is left heart failure. If you see JVD with clear lungs, think RV infarct, tamponade, PE, or lung disease. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Left vs right heart failure
slides.sub: How to tell them apart at the bedside

slides.title: The lungs back up
slides.sub: Blood damming up behind the pump
steps: Forward output falls and pressure builds behind it
Pressure backs up from the left atrium
Fluid crosses into the interstitium and alveoli

slides.title: The body backs up
steps: Most often from left heart failure
Pressure builds in the vena cava

slides.title: Findings side by side
cols: CXR: Kerley B lines, cephalization, effusions

slides.title: What usually causes each
slides.sub: Isolated right failure points to the lungs or pulmonary vessels
items: Hypertension, ischemic heart disease, aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, cardiomyopathy
Left heart failure (most common), cor pulmonale from COPD, PE, pulmonary hypertension

slides.title: Do not get fooled
items: Think RV infarct, tamponade, PE, or tension pneumothorax
Supports heart failure but also rises with PE, AF, and kidney disease
Look for the trigger: ischemia, arrhythmia, hypertensive surge, missed meds

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Left failure backs blood into the lungs: dyspnea, crackles, orthopnea. Right failure backs blood into the body: JVD, liver congestion, leg edema. Right failure with clear lungs? Hunt for a lung or pulmonary vessel cause, RV infarct, or tamponade.

caption: The body tries to rescue a failing heart, and the rescue makes things worse. Low output triggers sympathetic and RAAS activation, which raises preload and afterload and drives remodeling. That is why ACE inhibitors, ARBs, ARNIs, beta blockers, and MRAs improve survival in HFrEF. Loop diuretics relieve congestion but do not improve mortality. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Why the failing heart makes itself worse
The vicious cycle
steps: The brain thinks the patient is volume depleted
The heart works harder against more load
Dilation and fibrosis, a weaker pump

slides.title: Each rescue has a cost
items: Raises heart rate and contractility, but also oxygen demand and arrhythmia risk
Angiotensin II constricts vessels and aldosterone holds salt: more preload and afterload
Chronic stretch and angiotensin cause fibrosis and dilation

slides.title: Each drug breaks the cycle
items: Block angiotensin II: less afterload and remodeling
Blocks aldosterone: less fluid and fibrosis
Fewer HF hospitalizations in HFrEF and HFpEF

slides.title: Why do they decompensate
items: Ischemia, AF with RVR, nonadherence, infection, uncontrolled hypertension, high sodium intake
Warm or cold, wet or dry
Cold and wet patients are the sickest: low perfusion plus congestion

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Heart failure is a cycle: low output triggers sympathetic and RAAS activation, which adds load and remodeling. Modern therapy blocks the cycle. Diuretics relieve symptoms, neurohormonal blockers improve survival.

caption: An asthma attack has two phases. The early phase starts in minutes when allergen cross links IgE on mast cells and releases histamine and leukotrienes. The late phase starts hours later as Th2 cytokines recruit eosinophils and cause edema and mucus. Albuterol relaxes smooth muscle, inhaled steroids calm inflammation. A silent chest or a normal CO2 in a tiring patient is a danger sign. Save the last slide.

slides.title: What happens inside an asthma attack
slides.sub: Early phase, late phase, and why drugs work

slides.title: Hours later
slides.sub: The late response peaks about 6 to 8 hours after exposure
steps: Th2 cells release IL 4, IL 5, IL 13
Release proteins that damage the airway
Airways narrow again and become hyperreactive

slides.title: Mechanism to bedside
items: Narrowed airways make turbulent flow, loudest on expiration
Exhaling is hardest, so lungs hyperinflate and FEV1/FVC falls
Curschmann spirals (mucus casts) and Charcot Leyden crystals (eosinophil protein)

slides.title: Match the drug to the step
items: Beta 2 agonist: relaxes airway smooth muscle fast
Blocks muscarinic receptors: less vagal bronchoconstriction
Smooth muscle relaxation in severe attacks

slides.title: When the attack is winning
items: Little air moving is ominous, not reassuring
Early asthma hyperventilates, so a normal CO2 means fatigue

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Early phase is mast cells and bronchospasm, late phase is eosinophils and inflammation. Beta agonists open the airway now, steroids calm the inflammation. A quiet chest and a normal CO2 in a struggling patient mean trouble.

caption: DKA starts with insulin deficiency. Glucose cannot enter cells while fat breakdown makes ketoacids, causing an anion gap metabolic acidosis. Osmotic diuresis dehydrates the patient and depletes total body potassium even if the serum level looks normal or high. Fluids first, check potassium, then insulin. If potassium is low, replace it before starting insulin. Save the last slide.

slides.title: From no insulin to acidosis
steps: Plus fat breakdown into free fatty acids

slides.title: Serum K can lie to you
items: Serum K may look normal or high
Acidosis and insulin lack shift K out of cells
Serum K can crash on treatment
If K is low, replace it first, then start insulin

slides.title: What goes first
steps: Add dextrose when glucose falls below 250
So insulin can keep running until ketosis resolves

slides.title: In the ED
items: Infection, MI, missed insulin, new onset, SGLT2 inhibitor use (euglycemic DKA)
The goal is a closed gap
Cerebral edema is rare but mostly seen in children

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: No insulin means no glucose uptake and runaway ketone production. Treat the dehydration, respect the potassium, and use insulin until the anion gap closes.

caption: Nephrotic syndrome is a protein leak: proteinuria over 3.5 g/day, low albumin, edema, high lipids. Nephritic syndrome is glomerular inflammation: hematuria with RBC casts, hypertension, and azotemia. The classic nephrotic causes are minimal change (kids), FSGS, membranous, and diabetes. Classic nephritic causes are poststreptococcal GN, IgA nephropathy, and RPGN. Save the last slide.

slides.title: The leak
steps: The filter loses its charge or structure
Clots (loss of antithrombin III) and infections

slides.title: Know these four
items: Most common in children, foot process effacement, steroid responsive
Adults, anti PLA2R, spike and dome

slides.title: Know these three
items: Weeks after strep, low C3, lumpy bumpy immunofluorescence
Hematuria within days of an upper respiratory infection
Crescents on biopsy, anti GBM, ANCA, or immune complex

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Nephrotic means the filter leaks protein: edema, low albumin, clot risk. Nephritic means the filter is inflamed: blood in the urine, hypertension, rising creatinine.

caption: Shock is inadequate oxygen delivery. BP equals cardiac output times systemic vascular resistance. Hypovolemic shock is cold with low filling pressures, cardiogenic is cold and wet, distributive is warm with low SVR, and obstructive comes from PE, tamponade, or tension pneumothorax. Match the type to the fix. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Why pressure falls
steps: Perfusion does not meet oxygen demand

slides.title: The pattern for each type
items: CO down, SVR up, wedge down. Cold and dry
CO down, SVR up, wedge up. Cold and wet
SVR down, CO usually up in sepsis. Warm
CO down, SVR up or normal, wedge depends on the cause

slides.title: Fix the mechanism
items: Stop the loss, give blood for hemorrhage
Treat the cause, inotrope or pressor, careful with fluids
Fluids, antibiotics in sepsis, norepinephrine, epinephrine for anaphylaxis
Decompress, drain, or lyse the obstruction

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Ask four questions: is there enough volume, is the pump working, are the vessels tight or leaky, and is something blocking flow. The answer picks the treatment.

caption: STEMI in the ED: ECG within 10 minutes of first medical contact, activate the cath lab on ST elevation in two contiguous leads, give aspirin and an anticoagulant, and reperfuse. Primary PCI is preferred if it can happen within 120 minutes of first medical contact. Otherwise give fibrinolytics within 30 minutes and transfer. Inferior STEMI: get a right sided ECG before nitrates. Save the last slide.

slides.title: The sequence
steps: Get an ECG within 10 minutes of first medical contact

slides.title: One decision
items: Primary PCI, goal 90 minutes door to device

slides.title: Leads map to arteries
items: Posterior: confirm with V7 to V9

slides.title: RCA territory
items: Preload dependent: avoid nitrates, give fluids
The RCA supplies the AV node

slides.title: Absolute contraindications
items: Suspected aortic dissection, active bleeding, or BP over 180/110 unresponsive to treatment
Malignant intracranial tumor or known cerebrovascular malformation

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: ECG in 10 minutes, activate the cath lab, aspirin and heparin, and choose PCI or lytics by the 120 minute rule. In inferior STEMI check the right side before giving nitrates.

caption: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes is an emergency. Step 1: IV calcium to stabilize the heart. Step 2: shift potassium into cells with insulin and dextrose, albuterol, and bicarbonate if acidotic. Step 3: remove it with loop diuretics, binders, or dialysis. Calcium does not lower potassium, and shifts wear off, so plan for removal. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Real or fake
steps: Hemolysis can cause a false high
Peaked T waves, wide QRS, flat P waves, sine wave
Treat now, do not wait for a repeat

slides.title: Three steps
steps: Insulin with dextrose, albuterol, bicarbonate if acidotic

slides.title: Mechanism
items: Restores the gap to threshold potential and calms the myocardium
Drive Na K ATPase and move K into cells (10 units regular insulin IV)
Beta 2 stimulation of the pump (10 to 20 mg nebulized)

slides.title: Why you still need step 3
items: Works in minutes, lasts 30 to 60 minutes
Work in 15 to 30 minutes, last a few hours
Definitive when kidneys cannot clear it

slides.title: Do not stop at the number
items: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, trimethoprim, NSAIDs

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Calcium protects the heart, insulin and albuterol hide the potassium, and diuretics, binders, or dialysis get rid of it. Watch for hypoglycemia after insulin.

caption: Metabolic acidosis starts with the anion gap: sodium minus chloride minus bicarbonate. A high gap means unmeasured acids: methanol, uremia, DKA, propylene glycol or isoniazid or iron, lactate, ethylene glycol, salicylates. A normal gap means bicarbonate loss or chloride gain: diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis, saline. Save the last slide.

slides.title: MUDPILES
items: Methanol, uremia, DKA and other ketoacidosis

slides.title: Bicarbonate gone
items: Kidney cannot make or reabsorb bicarbonate

slides.title: Clues and treatment
slides.sub: Osmolar gap is high early and falls as the parent alcohol is metabolized

slides.title: A mixed picture
items: Respiratory alkalosis plus anion gap metabolic acidosis
Tinnitus, tachypnea, fever, altered mental status
Sodium bicarbonate and dialysis in severe cases. Be careful with intubation

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Calculate the gap first. High gap means an unmeasured acid, so think MUDPILES. Normal gap means lost bicarbonate, so think diarrhea and renal tubular acidosis.

caption: Acute stroke in the ED: note last known well, get a stat noncontrast CT and a glucose, then decide on reperfusion. Thrombolysis (tenecteplase or alteplase) works within 4.5 hours if there is no hemorrhage and BP is under 185/110, and the 2026 guideline allows selected patients up to 24 hours based on imaging. Thrombectomy is for large vessel occlusion. Hypoglycemia, postictal paralysis, and posterior circulation strokes are common traps. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Fast and in order
steps: Note the last known well time

slides.title: Tenecteplase or alteplase
items: Within 4.5 hours of last known well
Up to 24 hours in selected patients with salvageable brain on advanced imaging (2026 guideline)
Except glucose, and INR if on warfarin

slides.title: Do not give lytics if
items: Major surgery, trauma, or stroke within 3 months
DOAC within 48 hours or INR over 1.7

slides.title: Large vessel occlusion
items: ICA or proximal MCA on CT angiography
Up to 6 hours, up to 24 hours in selected patients

slides.title: Look alikes and misses
items: Vertigo and ataxia can look benign. Use a careful exam and HINTS

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Last known well, CT, glucose, then lysis if eligible (4.5 hours, longer in selected patients by imaging) and thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion. Control the BP and do not miss the mimics.

caption: PE workup depends on stability and pretest probability. Unstable patients get bedside echo and treatment. Low risk patients who are PERC negative need no testing. Others get D dimer, then CTPA if positive, and high probability goes straight to CTPA. Anticoagulate if stable, lyse if massive. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Risk stratify first
items: Bedside echo for RV strain, treat if suspected
D dimer, then CTPA if positive

slides.title: All must be absent
slides.sub: Use only if pretest probability is low
items: Age 50 or older, HR 100 or more, SpO2 under 95 percent
Unilateral leg swelling, hemoptysis, recent surgery or trauma
Prior PE or DVT, estrogen use

slides.title: Match to severity
items: Anticoagulation with heparin or a DOAC

slides.title: Details that matter
items: Sinus tachycardia is most common, S1Q3T3 is rare
Elevation marks RV strain and higher risk
D dimer rises normally, use a pregnancy specific pathway

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Stability first, then probability. Rule out with PERC or D dimer when low risk, image when not, anticoagulate, and lyse the unstable.

caption: Hyponatremia: check serum osmolality first, then volume status, then urine sodium and osmolality. SIADH is a euvolemic cause with high urine sodium. Severe symptoms like seizures get 3 percent saline in boluses. Correct slowly: overcorrection causes osmotic demyelination. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Three questions
steps: Normal or high suggests glucose, mannitol, or lab artifact

slides.title: Causes by group
items: Vomiting, diarrhea, diuretics, third spacing, adrenal insufficiency
SIADH, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, primary polydipsia, low solute intake

slides.title: The classic euvolemic cause
items: ADH keeps working despite low osmolality: free water retained
Low serum osmolality, urine osmolality over 100, urine sodium over 40
Small cell lung cancer, CNS disease, pneumonia, SSRIs, carbamazepine

slides.title: Symptoms drive treatment
items: Seizure, coma, herniation from cerebral edema
3 percent saline bolus (100 to 150 mL), repeat up to 3 times

slides.title: Do not overshoot
items: Under 8 to 10 mEq/L in 24 hours, 8 or less if high risk
Osmotic demyelination: dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis days later
Alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hypokalemia, chronic hyponatremia

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Osmolality, then volume status, then urine studies. Treat severe symptoms with 3 percent saline, correct slowly, and watch the sodium every few hours.

caption: The Hs and Ts are the reversible causes the AHA tells you to treat during every cardiac arrest: hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion, hypo and hyperkalemia, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, and pulmonary and coronary thrombosis. Think of them every 2 minutes, especially in PEA and asystole. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Volume, oxygen, acid
items: Fluids or blood, and look for the source of loss
Ventilate with high flow oxygen and confirm the airway is in the right place
Fix ventilation first, consider bicarbonate if the pH is severely low

slides.title: Potassium and temperature
items: IV calcium, insulin with dextrose, bicarbonate, albuterol
Active internal rewarming. If core temp is under 30 C, limit shocks and hold drugs until warmer

slides.title: Pressure and poisons
items: Decompress the chest, then place a chest tube
Treat the specific poison: naloxone if a pulse is present in opioid overdose, bicarbonate for sodium channel blockers, lipid emulsion for local anesthetic toxicity, digoxin Fab for digoxin

slides.title: Thrombosis
items: Systemic thrombolysis if PE is known or suspected, continue CPR
Emergent cath for STEMI after ROSC, consider ECPR in selected patients

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Every 2 minutes, while compressions continue, ask which H or T this could be. PEA and asystole are where they matter most. Ultrasound and the ECG find most of them fast.

caption: ECG pearl: T wave inversions in V1 to V4 and the inferior leads at the same time point to right heart strain, so think pulmonary embolism. Sinus tachycardia is still the most common PE finding, and a normal ECG does not rule it out. Save the last slide.

slides.title: T wave inversions in V1 to V4 and the inferior leads?
What it looks like
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real tracing

slides.title: Answer
slides.text: Think pulmonary embolism.

slides.title: What to know
items: Simultaneous T wave inversions in II, III, aVF and V1 to V4 reflect right ventricular strain
This combination is one of the most specific ECG findings for PE
Sinus tachycardia is the most common abnormality, and S1Q3T3 is the classic but less common sign
ACS is rarely tachycardic, so tachycardia plus this pattern favors PE

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Right heart strain on the ECG should make you think PE. Risk stratify with the Wells score, then D dimer or CTPA, and look at troponin and RV size if the patient is sick.

caption: ECG pearl: biphasic or deeply inverted T waves in V2 and V3 in a pain free patient with recent chest pain is Wellens syndrome, a sign of critical proximal LAD stenosis. Do not stress test these patients. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Pain free patient with deeply inverted or biphasic T waves in V2 and V3?
What it looks like
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real tracing

slides.title: Answer
slides.text: Wellens syndrome: critical proximal LAD stenosis.

slides.title: What to know
items: The pattern appears in the pain free window, often after chest pain has resolved
Troponin is normal or only slightly elevated
Biphasic T waves (type A) or deep symmetric inversion (type B, about 75 percent)
Little or no ST elevation and preserved R wave progression

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Do not stress test. Treat as unstable angina with a critical LAD lesion, admit, and arrange early angiography. The T waves can evolve into an anterior STEMI.

caption: ECG pearl: upsloping ST depression flowing into tall, symmetric T waves in the precordial leads is the de Winter pattern, a STEMI equivalent from proximal LAD occlusion. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Upsloping ST depression in the precordial leads with tall, symmetric T waves?
What it looks like
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real tracing

slides.title: Answer
slides.text: de Winter pattern: a STEMI equivalent from proximal LAD occlusion.

slides.title: What to know
items: Upsloping ST depression at the J point running into tall, symmetric T waves
Precordial leads, often with slight ST elevation in aVR
There is no classic ST elevation, so it is easy to miss
An acute occlusion, not an NSTEMI

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Tall T waves with upsloping ST depression in the chest leads in a patient with chest pain means call the cath lab. Do not wait for troponin.

caption: ECG pearl: horizontal ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves and upright T waves in a patient with chest pain suggests a posterior MI. Get posterior leads V7 to V9 to confirm. Save the last slide.

slides.title: ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves and upright T waves?
What it looks like
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real tracing

slides.title: Answer
slides.text: Posterior MI until proven otherwise.

slides.title: What to know
items: V1 to V3 look at the back wall from the front, so ST elevation shows up as ST depression and Q waves show up as tall R waves
Often with inferior or lateral infarction
Posterior leads V7 to V9: ST elevation of 0.5 mm or more confirms it

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Chest pain with horizontal ST depression in V1 to V3 means get posterior leads. If they show ST elevation, activate the cath lab.

caption: ECG pearl: ST elevation in aVR with widespread ST depression suggests left main or three vessel disease, or a demand state. It is a high risk pattern, not a routine NSTEMI. Save the last slide.

slides.title: ST elevation in aVR with diffuse ST depression?
What it looks like
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real tracing

slides.title: Answer
slides.text: Think left main or multivessel disease.

slides.title: What to know
items: ST elevation in aVR (often V1 too) with ST depression of 1 mm or more in eight or more leads
Severe ischemia from left main or three vessel disease, or a demand state
It looks at the heart from the right shoulder, the opposite direction of the left ventricle, so it mirrors diffuse subendocardial ischemia

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: This is a high risk ECG. Treat the patient as unstable, repeat ECGs, and involve cardiology early for angiography.

caption: ECG pearl: in LBBB or a paced rhythm, use the Smith modified Sgarbossa criteria: concordant ST elevation, concordant ST depression in V1 to V3, or ST elevation of at least 25 percent of the preceding S wave. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Chest pain with a left bundle branch block. How do you spot a STEMI?
What it looks like
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real tracing

slides.title: Answer
slides.text: Use the Smith modified Sgarbossa criteria.

slides.title: What to know
items: 1 mm or more in any lead, ST moving the same direction as the QRS
1 mm or more in V1, V2, or V3
1 mm or more and at least 25 percent of the depth of the preceding S wave
Any one is positive for the modified rule. The original needs a score of 3

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: In LBBB or a ventricular paced rhythm, look for ST changes that go with the QRS or are too big for the S wave. A positive rule means treat as occlusion MI.

caption: ECG pearl: sinus tachycardia, low voltage, and electrical alternans together point to cardiac tamponade. Confirm with bedside echo and drain if unstable. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Tachycardia, low voltage, and QRS height changing beat to beat?
What it looks like
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real tracing

slides.title: Answer
slides.text: Think cardiac tamponade.

slides.title: What to know
items: Sinus tachycardia, low QRS voltage, and electrical alternans
The heart swings in the effusion, so QRS height alternates every beat
JVD, hypotension, and muffled heart sounds (Beck triad)
Bedside echo: pericardial effusion with RV or RA collapse

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Obstructive shock with this ECG means get an echo now. If the patient is unstable, drain it with pericardiocentesis.

caption: ECG pearl: a very fast, irregular, wide complex rhythm with changing QRS shapes can be atrial fibrillation with WPW. Avoid AV nodal blockers. Cardiovert if unstable, procainamide if stable. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Very fast irregular wide complex tachycardia with varying QRS widths?
What it looks like
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real tracing

slides.title: Answer
slides.text: Atrial fibrillation with WPW. Do not give AV nodal blockers.

slides.title: What to know
items: The accessory pathway bypasses the AV node, so the ventricles can fire at 200 to 300 per minute and degenerate to VF
Digoxin, adenosine, calcium channel blockers, and beta blockers can speed conduction down the pathway

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: A wide, irregular, very fast rhythm in a young patient is pre-excited AF until proven otherwise. Cardiovert if unstable and keep the AV nodal blockers away.

caption: ECG pearl: coved ST elevation of at least 2 mm in V1 or V2 followed by an inverted T wave is the Brugada type 1 pattern. Fever and sodium channel blockers can unmask it. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Coved ST elevation in V1 and V2 followed by an inverted T wave?
What it looks like
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real tracing

slides.title: Answer
slides.text: Brugada type 1 pattern.

slides.title: What to know
items: Coved ST elevation of at least 2 mm in V1 or V2, followed by a negative T wave
Saddleback patterns are suggestive but not diagnostic
Fever, sodium channel blockers, cocaine, and alcohol can unmask it
Recording V1 and V2 one or two spaces higher can reveal it

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: A type 1 pattern with syncope or arrest needs admission and electrophysiology input. Treat fever and avoid triggering drugs. The definitive treatment is an ICD.

caption: ECG pearl: diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, and PR elevation in aVR, points to pericarditis. Reciprocal ST depression or convex ST elevation favors a STEMI instead. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Chest pain with diffuse concave ST elevation?
What it looks like
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real tracing

slides.title: Answer
slides.text: Think pericarditis, and check it is not a STEMI.

slides.title: What to know
items: Diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression, and PR elevation with ST depression in aVR
ST depression anywhere except aVR and V1 favors MI
Convex or tombstone ST elevation strongly favors MI
Sinus tachycardia, pericardial effusion on echo, and troponin if myocarditis is possible

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression is pericarditis. If any lead shows convex ST elevation or reciprocal depression, treat it as an MI.

caption: ECG pearl: polymorphic VT with a twisting QRS and a long QT is torsades de pointes. IV magnesium is first line, correct potassium, and stop QT prolonging drugs. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Twisting polymorphic VT with a long QT?
What it looks like
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real tracing

slides.title: Answer
slides.text: Torsades de pointes. Give magnesium.

slides.title: What to know
items: A short, long, short RR sequence leads into torsades, and the QT before it is long
Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV (about 25 to 30 mg/kg for a 70 to 80 kg adult), even with a normal magnesium level
Stop QT prolonging drugs and correct potassium
Pulseless torsades gets defibrillated. Pacing or isoproterenol can raise the heart rate

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Long QT plus polymorphic VT means magnesium, fix potassium, and stop the offending drug. Shock it if the patient is pulseless or unstable.

caption: ECG pearl: treat a wide complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise. AV dissociation, capture or fusion beats, and chest lead negative concordance point to VT, and stable vitals do not rule it out. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Regular wide complex tachycardia in a patient who looks stable?
What it looks like
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real tracing

slides.title: Answer
slides.text: Treat it as VT until proven otherwise.

slides.title: What to know
items: Most wide complex tachycardias are VT, especially in patients over 35 or with heart disease
AV dissociation, capture or fusion beats, and negative concordance in the chest leads
A normal blood pressure does not rule out VT

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: When you are unsure, call it VT. Look for AV dissociation and fusion beats, and do not be reassured by a stable blood pressure.

caption: ECG pearl: inferior STEMI with hypotension, JVD, and clear lungs is an RV infarct until proven otherwise. Get a right sided ECG and avoid nitrates. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Inferior STEMI with hypotension, JVD, and clear lungs?
What it looks like
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real tracing

slides.title: Answer
slides.text: Right ventricular infarct. Get V4R and avoid nitrates.

slides.title: What to know
items: RV infarction complicates up to 40 percent of inferior STEMIs
ST elevation in III greater than II, or ST elevation in V1 with ST depression in V2
ST elevation of 1 mm in V4R (sensitivity 88 percent, specificity 78 percent)
Avoid nitrates, diuretics, and opioids. Give gentle fluids and reperfuse

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Every inferior STEMI deserves a right sided ECG. If the RV is involved, protect the preload and go for reperfusion.

caption: ECG pearl: scooped ST segments are the digitalis effect and do not mean toxicity. Toxicity shows up as arrhythmias like atrial tachycardia with block or bidirectional VT. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Scooped ST segments on an ECG in a patient taking digoxin?
What it looks like
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real tracing

slides.title: Answer
slides.text: Digitalis effect, not toxicity.

slides.title: What to know
items: Scooped ST segments (the reverse tick) occur at therapeutic levels
Arrhythmias: frequent PVCs, atrial tachycardia with block, AF with a slow regular response, bidirectional VT
High potassium in acute toxicity marks severe poisoning
Digoxin Fab for life threatening arrhythmias or severe hyperkalemia

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Scooped ST segments mean the patient is on digoxin, not poisoned by it. Toxicity is a clinical picture plus arrhythmias, so treat the patient and not the level.

caption: ECG pearl: low calcium lengthens the QT interval and high calcium shortens it. Low potassium and low magnesium also cause long QT patterns and torsades risk. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Long QT or short QT: which electrolyte?
What it looks like
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real tracing

slides.title: Answer
slides.text: Low calcium lengthens the QT. High calcium shortens it.

slides.title: What to know
items: It controls the ST segment length, so low calcium means a long QT and high calcium means a short QT
Flat T waves, U waves, and a long QU interval that can be mistaken for a long QT
Long QT with a risk of torsades
Tall, peaked T waves are the earliest sign

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Check calcium, potassium, and magnesium in any patient with a long QT before you give a QT prolonging drug.

caption: Anaphylaxis is IgE mediated mast cell and basophil degranulation. Histamine and other mediators cause vasodilation, leak, and bronchospasm. Epinephrine IM into the anterolateral thigh is first line. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts only. Observe for a biphasic reaction. Save the last slide.

slides.title: How it happens
steps: IgE binds mast cells and basophils

slides.title: Skin plus one more system
items: Vomiting, cramping after a likely allergen

slides.title: Epinephrine first
items: 0.01 mg/kg, usually 0.3 to 0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL in adults, anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 to 15 minutes
Airway, oxygen, IV fluids, lie flat
H1 and H2 blockers and steroids come after epinephrine
Still give epinephrine, glucagon if refractory

slides.title: Do not discharge too fast
items: Can recur hours later, so observe 4 to 12 hours based on risk
Epinephrine auto-injector and an action plan
Can support the diagnosis if unclear

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Anaphylaxis is mast cell degranulation. Give IM epinephrine early, support the airway and circulation, and observe for a biphasic reaction.

caption: Sepsis in the ED: measure lactate, get cultures, give broad antibiotics within 1 hour if shock is likely or present, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypoperfusion, and start norepinephrine for a MAP under 65 despite fluids. Source control matters too. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Sepsis first hours
slides.sub: What to do and in what order

slides.title: The sequence
steps: Blood cultures before antibiotics if no delay
Within 1 hour for septic shock or high likelihood
30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate 4 or higher

slides.title: If still hypotensive
items: Vasopressin if the norepinephrine dose keeps climbing
Reassess volume status and perfusion with dynamic measures

slides.title: Beyond bugs and drugs
items: Drain the abscess, remove the infected device
Without shock, 3 hours after a quick workup is acceptable if infection is still likely

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Sepsis is time sensitive: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, pressors if needed, and find the source.

caption: Aortic dissection: sudden tearing pain, pulse or blood pressure differences, neuro deficits, or a new aortic regurgitation murmur. Use the ADD-RS, then CT angiography. Control heart rate first with a beta blocker, then blood pressure. Type A goes to surgery. Save the last slide.

slides.title: High risk clues
items: Sudden, severe, tearing, chest or back
Pulse deficit, arm BP difference, new diastolic murmur, focal neuro deficit
It is often misdiagnosed as an MI

slides.title: From suspicion to answer
steps: D-dimer may help in low or intermediate risk
CT angiography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis
If the patient is too unstable for CT

slides.title: Anti-impulse therapy
items: Beta blocker such as esmolol, goal below 60
Treat it, since pain drives pressure
Type A: emergency surgery. Type B: medical management unless complicated

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Think of dissection with tearing pain and pulse or BP differences. Image with CT angiography, control heart rate before blood pressure, and call surgery for type A.

caption: Upper GI bleed in the ED: resuscitate, risk stratify with the Glasgow-Blatchford score, transfuse for hemoglobin of 7 or less, start an IV PPI, and get endoscopy within 24 hours. If varices are possible, add octreotide and ceftriaxone. Save the last slide.

slides.title: First steps
steps: CBC, type and screen, coags, BUN, liver tests
Glasgow-Blatchford: very low risk patients may go home

slides.title: Start early
items: Pantoprazole 80 mg bolus, then continuous or intermittent dosing

slides.title: Find and fix
items: Especially in cirrhosis, since it can raise portal pressure
Admit unless Blatchford score is 0 to 1

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Upper GI bleed: resuscitate, transfuse at 7, give a PPI, add octreotide and ceftriaxone for varices, and scope within 24 hours.

caption: AF with RVR in the ED: unstable patients get synchronized cardioversion. Stable patients get rate control with a beta blocker or diltiazem, or rhythm control. Avoid diltiazem in systolic heart failure. In WPW, use cardioversion or procainamide. Decide on anticoagulation with CHA2DS2-VASc. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Stable or not?
steps: Hypotension, ischemia, pulmonary edema, altered mentation
Choose rate control or rhythm control

slides.title: Common choices
items: Diltiazem, but avoid in reduced ejection fraction
Use caution with all negative inotropes
AV nodal blockers can speed pathway conduction

slides.title: Cardioversion in the ED
items: Consider cardioversion in low risk patients

slides.title: Do not skip it
items: Direct oral anticoagulants are first line

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Unstable AF gets shocked. Stable AF gets rate or rhythm control. Think about heart failure, WPW, and anticoagulation.

caption: Chest pain in the ED: rule out the life threats before you think about benign causes. These are acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection, tension pneumothorax, and esophageal rupture. Each has one clue and one test. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Must not miss
items: Pleuritic pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, risk factors
Tearing pain, pulse or BP difference
Absent breath sounds, hypotension, tracheal deviation
Severe pain after vomiting or instrumentation

slides.title: Fast and cheap
items: Within 10 minutes for high risk chest pain

slides.title: Based on suspicion
items: Wells score, D-dimer, CT pulmonary angiography
Needle or chest tube if tension

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Run the big five first. Each one has a clue, a test, and a time sensitive fix.

caption: FTW² (For the Wards, For the Win): the PEG tube. A PEG is a tube placed through the abdominal wall into the stomach under endoscopic guidance, held in place by an internal bumper and an external bolster. It is used when a patient needs enteral access for more than 4 to 6 weeks. Know the early and late complications, and never blindly replace a tube from the first month. Save the last slide.

slides.tag: FTW² · FOR THE WARDS, FOR THE WIN
slides.title: What is a PEG tube? What to know
slides.sub: Description, function, and what goes wrong

slides.title: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy
items: Passes through the abdominal wall into the stomach
An internal bumper sits against the stomach wall and an external bolster rests on the skin
Stomach wall seals to the abdominal wall around it. It matures in about 1 to 2 weeks and is well formed by about 4 weeks
Enteral access needed for more than 4 to 6 weeks

slides.title: What it does and who gets one
items: Feeds, fluids, and liquid meds go straight into the stomach, bypassing the mouth and esophagus. It can also decompress the stomach
Head and neck or esophageal cancer
Everything distal to the stomach must function

slides.title: Contraindications
items: Poor tract formation and leak risk
Or bowel obstruction when used for feeding

slides.title: First weeks after placement
items: The tract has not matured yet

slides.title: Months later
items: Most common. Poor flushing or crushed meds
Leaking around the site, moist red tissue
The internal bumper migrates into the tract. Tube will not rotate or advance, or feeds hurt
Bumper can lodge in the pylorus and cause gastric outlet obstruction

slides.title: Do not force it
items: Gentle push and pull with a 30 to 60 mL syringe
Clamp for 15 to 20 minutes, then repeat
Use a wire, and do not force it
Flush 15 to 30 mL before and after meds and after feeds

slides.title: First question: how old is the tract?
items: Do not replace blindly. It risks placement into the peritoneum, so get surgery or GI involved
Replace it promptly. A mature tract can close within hours
A same size or smaller Foley can hold the tract open until replacement
Check placement before feeding, with a contrast study if there is doubt

slides.title: Prevent aspiration
items: Head of bed at least 30 degrees during feeds and 30 to 60 minutes after
Give separately, in liquid form when possible, with flushes between
Put fiber supplements through the tube

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: A PEG is a stomach tube through the abdominal wall. Clogs are the most common problem, and the first question on a dislodged tube is how old the tract is.

caption: FTW² (For the Wards, For the Win): how to spike and prime an IV bag. Close the roller clamp, spike the bag with a twist while keeping the spike and port sterile, hang it, fill the drip chamber one third to one half full, then slowly prime the tubing and clear the air before connecting to the patient. Save the last slide.

slides.tag: FTW² · FOR THE WARDS, FOR THE WIN
slides.title: How to spike and prime an IV bag
Set up
items: Then gather the bag, tubing, and a basin or sink
Right fluid, not expired, clear, no leaks
Take it out of the package and keep both ends sterile

slides.title: Close the clamp first
items: Just below the drip chamber, about 3 cm
So fluid cannot run through when you spike

slides.title: Spike the bag
items: On the bag port and on the tubing spike. Do not touch either one
About 1 meter above the IV site for gravity flow

slides.title: Fill the drip chamber
items: Until it is one third to one half full
Fluid in the chamber keeps air out of the tubing
Follow the device instructions for its set

slides.title: Prime the line
items: Hold the tubing end over a basin or sink
Invert the Y ports and back check valves as fluid passes so air escapes
Fluid drips from the end and the whole line is full

slides.title: Before it touches the patient
items: To push bubbles out, or prime again
Air in the line can cause an air embolism. Very tiny bubbles are tolerated
Clamp, recap the end, and label the bag and tubing

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Clamp closed, spike with a twist, fill the chamber, prime slowly, check for air, and never touch the spike or port.

caption: FTW² (For the Wards, For the Win): neuro exam pearls. Go in order: mental status, cranial nerves, motor, reflexes, sensory, cerebellar, and gait. Localize first, grade strength 0 to 5, and sort upper from lower motor neuron signs. Save the last slide.

slides.tag: FTW² · FOR THE WARDS, FOR THE WIN
slides.title: Neuro exam pearls
slides.sub: Bedside order and what the findings mean

slides.title: Eight steps
items: Motor, then reflexes including special reflexes like Babinski

slides.title: Localize before you examine
items: So you know what you expect to find
A good neuro exam is not a 5 minute exam
Examine off sedation if it is safe to pause it

slides.title: Language and thought
items: Can they name objects and speak smoothly?
Can they follow a complex command?

slides.title: Grade 0 to 5
items: No movement, or a flicker of movement
Moves in the horizontal plane but not against gravity
4 is weak against resistance. 5 is full strength

slides.title: What to check
items: UMN pattern. Clonus is a 4+ response
Biceps C5 C6, triceps C6 C7, knee L2 to L4, ankle S1
Reinforce with the finger hooking maneuver if needed

slides.title: Cerebellar and gait
items: Finger to nose and heel to shin
An ataxic gait suggests a cerebellar lesion
Protrudes toward the side of the lesion

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Go in a set order, localize first, grade strength 0 to 5, and sort the findings into upper versus lower motor neuron.

caption: FTW² (For the Wards, For the Win): how to read a bedside monitor. Know what each tracing and number means, remember the blood pressure shown may not be current, and treat the patient before you trust the alarm. Save the last slide.

slides.tag: FTW² · FOR THE WARDS, FOR THE WIN
slides.title: How to read a bedside monitor
slides.sub: Top to bottom, and what to trust

slides.title: What you will see
items: The rhythm across the top with the HR number
Oxygen saturation with its pulse waveform
Cuff BP with MAP, or an arterial line waveform

slides.title: NIBP basics
items: Not always the current blood pressure. Press the button for a new one
The device measures MAP. Systolic and diastolic are derived

slides.title: Invasive blood pressure
items: A waveform from a catheter in an artery
Shows BP, HR, and MAP continuously
A damped or flat waveform can mean a bad reading or line problem

slides.title: When to distrust it
items: Atrial fibrillation or VT can confuse the sensor
A clean pulse waveform means a more trustworthy number

slides.title: Why they go off
items: ECG electrodes. One poor lead can set off many alarms
All can be affected by lead contact
Do not disable an alarm without telling the bedside nurse

slides.title: Look at the patient
items: Is the trace clean and the lead on?

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Read the ECG, SpO2, and pressure together. Check lead contact, cuff size, and the pleth before you trust any single number, and always look at the patient first.

caption: FTW² (For the Wards, For the Win): Foley catheters. Place one only for a real indication, keep the system closed with the bag below the bladder, review the need every day, and remove it as soon as you can to prevent CAUTI. Save the last slide.

slides.tag: FTW² · FOR THE WARDS, FOR THE WIN
slides.title: Foley catheters
slides.sub: When to place, when to pull

slides.title: Appropriate indications
items: Acute urinary retention or bladder outlet obstruction
Open sacral or perineal wound in an incontinent patient
Selected surgeries, prolonged immobilization, comfort at end of life

slides.title: Inappropriate uses
items: Not a substitute for nursing care
Not when the patient can void
Not for a long time without a reason

slides.title: Insert safely
items: Consistent with good drainage, to limit urethral trauma

slides.title: Daily care
items: Do not change the catheter or bag on a fixed schedule

slides.title: Remove early
items: Does it still have an indication?
Remove as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours

slides.title: Think before placing
items: For cooperative men without retention or obstruction
To confirm whether there is retention

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Every Foley needs a reason. Keep it closed and below the bladder, review it daily, and take it out as soon as the reason is gone.

caption: FTW² (For the Wards, For the Win): central lines. A central line ends in the superior vena cava or right atrium. Know the difference between a CVC, a PICC, a tunneled catheter, and a port, and remember a midline is not central. Save the last slide.

slides.tag: FTW² · FOR THE WARDS, FOR THE WIN
slides.title: Central lines: CVC, PICC, port
slides.sub: What each one is and why it matters

slides.title: The tip location
items: A catheter that ends in the SVC or right atrium
Mid to lower SVC, the cavoatrial junction, or high right atrium
Chest x-ray for the tip position

slides.title: Placed in the neck, chest, or groin
Placed through an arm vein
items: Basilic, brachial, cephalic, or median cubital
Right basilic: larger and the straightest path
Can be placed at the bedside without surgery
Ends in the SVC like any central line

slides.title: Long term access
items: Hickman, Broviac, and permanent dialysis catheters
Implanted under the skin of the chest, accessed with a needle
A port can stay in for years

slides.title: Midlines
items: A midline is not a PICC

slides.title: Common reasons
items: Repeated blood products, CVP monitoring, power injection of contrast

slides.title: What to watch for
items: Thrombosis or stenosis around the catheter
Tip too deep in the heart

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Central means the tip is in the SVC or right atrium. CVCs are short term, PICCs go through the arm, ports are implanted, and a midline is not central.

caption: FTW² (For the Wards, For the Win): oxygen delivery devices. Know the flow range and rough FiO2 of a nasal cannula, face mask, non-rebreather, Venturi mask, and high flow nasal cannula, and step up when the patient needs more. Save the last slide.

slides.tag: FTW² · FOR THE WARDS, FOR THE WIN
slides.title: Oxygen delivery devices
slides.sub: From nasal cannula to high flow

slides.title: Low flow
items: About 24% at 1 L/min, then roughly 4% more per liter up to about 44%
Above 4 to 6 L/min dries the nose
Mild or no distress. Patient can eat and talk

slides.title: Higher low flow
items: Exhaled CO2 can rebreathe in the mask
Hard to eat and talk with

slides.title: Reservoir bag
items: Flow must exceed the patient's demand
Severe hypoxemia while you arrange more support

slides.title: Precise FiO2
items: Air entrainment ports set the FiO2
When a controlled FiO2 matters, such as COPD

slides.title: Heated and humidified
items: Lowers work of breathing, flushes CO2, gives a little PEEP
Noninvasive ventilation or intubation if failing

slides.title: Step up as needed
items: Titrate to the patient and reassess

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Match the device to the need: nasal cannula for mild, masks for moderate, non-rebreather or high flow for severe, Venturi when you need a set FiO2.

caption: Cullen sign is bruising around the belly button and Grey Turner sign is bruising of the flanks. Both mean blood has tracked from the retroperitoneum under the skin. They are late, uncommon signs, classically seen in severe hemorrhagic pancreatitis, so look for the source of bleeding. Save the last slide.

slides.title: Cullen and Grey Turner signs
slides.sub: What they look like and why they happen

slides.title: Where the bruising shows up
slides.sub: Schematic drawing, not a real photograph

slides.title: What you see
items: Blue or purple discoloration around the umbilicus
Bruising of the flank, between the last rib and the top of the hip
Blue, purple, or brown, often turning green or yellow as it ages

slides.title: How blood reaches the skin
steps: Blood collects in the retroperitoneum or abdomen
Along the gastrohepatic and falciform ligaments to the umbilicus
From the posterior pararenal space to the flank

slides.title: Think bleeding, not just the pancreas
items: Severe acute necrotizing or hemorrhagic pancreatitis is the classic cause
Abdominal trauma, ruptured spleen, perforated duodenal ulcer, bleeding on anticoagulation

slides.title: A late and uncommon sign
items: Appears at least 24 hours after the bleeding starts
Absence does not rule out bleeding
In pancreatitis it points to severe disease

slides.title: What to do
items: Airway, breathing, circulation, and IV access
CBC, type and screen, coags, lipase, and hCG in women of reproductive age
Bedside ultrasound for free fluid and aorta, then CT if stable
Surgery, GI, or OB depending on the source

slides.title: Key takeaway
slides.text: Cullen is bruising around the navel and Grey Turner is bruising of the flanks. Both mean tracking blood. They are late signs, so find and treat the source of bleeding.
